UAP LAB · “Gimbal” Navy infrared video

Carrier-pilot ATFLIR footage (recorded 2015, released by the U.S. Navy in April 2020). Everything on this page marked measured was extracted from your file frame by frame; everything marked modelled rests on stated assumptions. The video alone cannot give the object’s true speed, and this page shows exactly why.

Object lock · 4× zoom thermal

Cropped around the tracked blob. Watch the white-hot → black-hot switch at ≈12.5 s and the turn of the shape after ≈25 s.

Sky-relative track measured

Path of the object against the clouds (px of image, y down). The pod keeps the object at screen centre, so any “motion” is really the camera slewing to hold it; the clouds are the only fixed reference in the frame.

Apparent orientation of the object

Sensor look angle (HUD) and its rate

Angle left (+) / right (−) of the jet’s nose, read from the on-screen “NN° L/R” every 2 s. Falling ≈1.8°/s on average, faster at the end. Orange: angle (plotted ×1.5). Blue: rate of change (plotted ×20, i.e. −2 on the axis ≈ −0.1°/s per unit).

Thermal signature: peak and background level

0–255 grey level, not temperature. The jump at ≈12.5 s is the operator switching polarity, not the object changing.

Apparent size and shape

Blob area in pixels (orange) and elongation (axis ratio, green ×100). A few hundred pixels ≈ a few pixels of true width: the object is small and heavily blurred, so shape details are unresolvable.

Speed lab modelled

Why no speed is measurable: one infrared camera measures angles, not distance. Observed: the line of sight swings ω (°/s) as read from the HUD. For an assumed range R, the object’s sideways speed relative to the line of sight is v⊥ = R·|ω| + v_jet·sin(look angle) (jet flying straight, ≈349 kt: Mach 0.58 at 25,010 ft ≈ 180 m/s). Slide R to see what each assumption implies.
Range
Moment
Lines: required sideways speed vs. range at three moments. Shaded bands mark the speed of a jet (≈0.5 Mach) and Mach 1. Take-away: inside ≈5 nmi the numbers are ordinary; at 20+ nmi the same angles would demand supersonic speed if the geometry is as assumed. This is exactly why range, not the video, decides the speed claim. Also note: with the jet flying straight, a stationary object would need R = v·sin(look)/ω ≈ 3 nmi at the start and shrinking toward 0 as the look angle nears 0, which is physically implausible, so either the object moves, the jet was banking/turning, or the line of sight is not simply nose-relative. The bank angle is not in the clip, so this cannot be closed from the video.

Competing explanations vs. what was measured

HypothesisFitsStrains
Distant conventional aircraft + IR glare (proposed by several independent analysts)Blob stays a constant tiny size; shape does not resolve; look-angle sweep consistent with a far object that is hardly closing; rotation can come from the pod’s image derotation when the look angle approaches 0°, which is exactly when the rotation starts here (≈25 s, look angle ≈10°→1°).Needs range/track data not in the clip; pilots’ radio chatter described unusual behaviour that the video can’t confirm.
Genuine anomalous craft (claimed by some witnesses/advocates)Apparent rotation of ≈110° in ≈9 s; no visible wings, exhaust or plume at this resolution.Rotation timing coincides with the sensor geometry; no independent radar track published; absence of features is expected at this pixel scale.
Sensor / processing artefactPolarity switch, gimbal slewing and auto-gain visibly change the picture (see signature chart).Does not by itself explain a persistent compact heat source.
Status: the U.S. Department of Defense released the clip as “unexplained” in 2020; AARO’s public reports describe no evidence of extraterrestrial technology. Treat the hypotheses as open, not settled.

The wider UAP picture · sightings data

AARO’s FY2024 report: how its 757 received reports were dispositioned.
Of cases AARO resolved, what they turned out to be (balloons dominate).
Sources (searched 4 Oct 2026): AARO FY2024 report as reported by NewsNation/ABC; AARO FY2025 consolidated report (published 20 July 2026) as summarised by The Black Vault and New Space Economy; NUFORC statistics via KSWB/Nexstar, Universe Today and local-press analyses. Annual AARO counts cover different windows and criteria, so don’t compare them as a trend. The first bar uses the “281 reports in the prior report” figure quoted by ABC.

Reading the numbers

Reports are not events. NUFORC takes unverified witness submissions (it filters obvious hoaxes only), so volume tracks awareness, media and Starlink/rocket launches as much as the sky; AARO itself attributes its jump from 281 to 757 reports to greater awareness and wider agency reporting. Resolution is lopsided toward the mundane: among resolved military cases, 70% were balloons, 16% drones, 8% birds, 4% satellites, 2% aircraft; most of the rest are “insufficient data”, which is a statement about the data, not the object. Residual cases (21 flagged for further investigation in FY2024; 191 sent to the FY2025 active archive) are where sensor artefacts, parallax, drones and genuinely unknown things all hide; the label “UAP” bundles causes that may share nothing. What would settle a case: calibrated multi-sensor data with range (radar + EO/IR + pod bank angle + jet track), which this clip lacks.

Method and limits

1,033 frames at 29.97 fps (34.5 s), 1280×720, sensor picture in the centre. Object: segmented inside the HUD bracket by local contrast against the median background (threshold adaptive to polarity); orientation/elongation from image moments; orientation unwrapped across the 180° ambiguity. Cloud drift: global phase correlation on the lower cloud area, frames with weak correlation zeroed, 5-frame smoothing, so the sky trail is indicative, not survey grade. HUD: look angle read by eye from enlarged crops every 2 s (automatic OCR was unreliable); altitude 25,010 ft and Mach 0.58 read from the display. Pixel values are display grey levels, not calibrated temperature. No claim here identifies the object.
